title: Astra for Coding: Why Are We Doing This Again?
author: manojbajaj95
tldr: Armin Ronacher let GPT 6 Astra run an unsupervised "software factory" for 35 hours and got 75k lines of unusable code. Ronacher argues the model is trained to finish long tasks and save tokens, not to write code a human can read, so it stops paying off for working software engineers.

keyPoints: Ronacher calls Astra impressive at computer use, images and long tasks, and borrows the Chinese idea of involution (neijuan) for AI engineering, where more and more effort goes in without more output per person.

Ronacher gave Astra one prompt, to build a Python with virtual threads and lexical scoping, and let it run its own workflow and subagents. After 35 hours, about 1B tokens, roughly $1,200 in API cost, 79 commits and 75k added lines, it had produced nothing of value and it never stopped on its own.

Astra skips the harness's edit tool and patches files, including C source in CPython, with dense one-line Python heredocs, and it chains Bash into Python into Node.js into PowerShell. A human can't follow these edits as they happen.

The same code-golf style leaks into committed code. The author shows tests with no whitespace discipline, several C macro calls on one line, magic integer indexes into a function table, and a probe function switching over 70 numbered cases that non-test code began to depend on.

Ronacher's theory is that training rewards task completion, token efficiency and simple metrics like cyclomatic complexity, with little penalty for unreadable code. Code that is bad by human standards may suit a codebase only agents read, which is why the author doubts these pricier models are aimed at software engineers at all.
article.whyItMatters: Anyone running long agent sessions or weighing Astra or Fable against cheaper models should look at the original for the code samples. The summary can describe the Python heredoc edits and the 70-case C switch, but seeing them makes the readability argument better than any description.

comments.overview: The thread mostly agreed with Ronacher and filled it out with complaints about Astra's cost, scope creep and Python-script edits. The longest fight was older than the model, though. Can you stop reading AI-written code and still ship maintainable software? Skeptics and people who say they do it daily argued that one through several long subthreads.

themes.title: Can you stop reading the code?
themes.synthesis: The top comment said bad code makes models slower to change it until progress stops, and that the people who claim they no longer read code rarely get past a proof of concept. Defenders described what works for them: small projects, clients who want speed over quality, strict module boundaries, heavy testing and review by more agents. Critics answered that this concedes the point, since those setups still catch bad patterns only when a human looks, and that the cost of the slowdown lands later and on teammates.

quotes.author: taurath
quotes.text: When the code is shitty it becomes harder and harder for the models to make changes and this grinds progress down to a halt

quotes.author: xgb84j
quotes.text: Work for business people who want fast results. Agentic coding gets you to something presentable much faster at the cost of code quality. I have never seen a customer or business person care about that.

themes.title: The Python edits come from the harness
themes.synthesis: Several people had seen Opus, Fable and Astra edit files through Python scripts too. Some blamed the harness. Commenters said Claude Code's auto mode prompt pushes the model toward Bash and Python, and that scripts save tokens when every tool call re-reads a large cached context. Others found scripted bulk edits less reliable than many plain edits, because the agent then spends time debugging its own script. A user who had asked Sol for scripted code moves saw Astra apply it to every edit, which makes the change harder to read.

quotes.author: klibertp
quotes.text: After switching to Astra, I saw it suddenly do this for all edits in all projects, which isn't great: the second argument to `replace` is still written "from memory", but now you need to unravel the Python script before you can understand what was actually changed.

quotes.author: IceDane
quotes.text: when I asked it why it kept editing code with python, it explained that this is part of its prompt when auto mode is turned on.

themes.title: Trained to finish, not to collaborate
themes.synthesis: Many backed Ronacher's training theory. The guess was that labs shifted reinforcement learning from human ratings toward long-horizon task completion, giving agents that finish more but talk and cooperate worse. Users reported Astra running full test suites over and over, writing its own tools instead of asking for a command, and taking six hours on a rebase Sol did in one. Some said it burned their subscription several times faster than Sol for no visible gain. A few suspected labs have little reason to make models write less code, while others replied that switching providers is easy enough to keep that in check.

quotes.author: nojs
quotes.text: My suspicion is that both OpenAI and Anthropic moved their RL agendas from "being rated as useful according to human feedback" to "succeeds at long horizon tasks" in the last few months, resulting in agents that are closer to AGI in an autonomous task-completing sense, but strangely bad at communicating.

quotes.author: AmazingTurtle
quotes.text: while gpt-5.6-sol consistently took like an hour to do so end-to-end, astra ran for more than 6 hours and still wasn't done. it kept finding "one more thing" that was goldplating that I didn't ask for.

themes.title: The compiler analogy doesn't hold
themes.synthesis: One commenter compared LLM output to compiled assembly that nobody reads. Most replies rejected it. A compiler is deterministic and works from a formally specified language, while a prompt is ambiguous English. Unlike a compiler, an agent also has to read its own output back and edit it, so the generated source is what it works in. A minority said the analogy works for throwaway build scripts and frontends where you only check the result.

quotes.author: recursivecaveat
quotes.text: Indeed, the compiler does not have to ingest its own output, figure it out, and insert modifications in the middle. Source code is the medium that LLMs work in.

themes.title: Short, specified tasks in a good codebase
themes.synthesis: People reporting good results described the opposite of Ronacher's experiment. They gave detailed specs, worked feature by feature and reviewed each step, often inside an established codebase whose patterns the agent copies. Others warned that bad code in context pulls the model toward more of it, and that writing specs that detailed costs almost as much as writing the code. Critics of the article added that a factory left to design its own workflow tests little that matters.

quotes.author: 0xpgm
quotes.text: An established codebase is already the best kind of context you could give an agent. It has all the patterns baked in so the agent simply follows established patterns.

quotes.author: juancn
quotes.text: Long horizon agents can degenerate at machine speed.

comments.consensus: Astra is capable but drifts badly when left alone for long. It writes code that is hard for humans to read and costs much more than Sol without clearly better results. Short, reviewed tasks still beat long autonomous runs.
comments.dissent: A sizable minority said they ship working software without reading most of the code, using boundaries, tests and agent review. Others called the article an outdated complaint that the next model will fix, or said its 35-hour single-prompt setup was bound to fail.

contrarian.author: ACCount37
contrarian.text: Unlike the usual causes of code rot (cheap replaceable developers, outsourcing to India), AI might actually get out of the pit - by getting good enough at refactoring to be able to beat the code back into shape. There's nothing about refactoring in particular that demands a meatbag when the rest of the coding tasks don't.
contrarian.why: The thread treated unmaintainable code as a new AI problem, while this comment points out that code rot is old and asks whether the same tools could also be the ones that clean it up.
